body_markdown:
The cybersecurity risks posed by AI took dramatic form recently through a villain with a sinister name: Jade Puffer. Security firm Sysdig applied that label to[a ransomware attack](https://siliconangle.com/2026/07/06/ai-agent-exploits-langflow-first-fully-autonomous-ransomware-attack/#:~:text=In%20the%20case%20researchers%20detail,the%20top%20of%20the%20scale.) in which a human initiated the operation but an autonomous[AI agent](https://www.salesforce.com/agentforce/ai-agents/?d=cta-body-promo-8) independently carried out the entire technical intrusion, from reconnaissance to database encryption and deletion.


As malicious actors increasingly deploy automation to execute attacks, organizations must defend themselves with AI agents built to detect and neutralize the threats. Because these intrusions happen in milliseconds — far too fast for human intervention — defenders must design agents they can trust not to go rogue. Call it the AI version of Spy vs. Spy.


“It can sound like cloak-and-dagger James Bond machinations,” said Muhammad Fraser-Rahim, Salesforce’s VP of Global Intelligence and Product/Platform Risk. “But this is the moment we are in, and I don’t think we necessarily have to be afraid of it.”


Greg Notch, CTO at cybersecurity company Expel, said agentic AI gives even low-skilled attackers sophisticated new weapons. But the technology also enables defenders to sift through the potential-attack alarms to identify the ones requiring action.
